- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts show gradual upward drift, cap the forecast slope or introduce early mean reversion if true price spikes then declines.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior 18-day avg), model tends to over-forecast continuation; reduce forecast slope by 15–25% for next 5–7 days.
- If official event net supply is strongly bearish (net < -15) and sentiment is neutral or bearish, model often under-estimates downside; add 3–5% downward bias to forecast mean.
- When sentiment history shows repeated 0.00 or low values (≤0.33), model tends to ignore recent volatility; force a 1–2% upward adjustment to forecast if true price deviates >5% from prior 18-day mean.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >10% from model’s 1st day forecast, apply a “lag correction” — adjust forecast by -0.5 to -1.0% per day for the next 5 days if price is trending down.
- If model forecasts are flat or rising slowly while sentiment is bullish, check for “overshoot bias” — if true price rises >15% from prior 18-day mean, reduce forecast by 2–3% for next 3 days.
- When official events are frequent (≥20/30d) and supply net is negative, model often over-optimistically forecasts upward trend; apply a “supply drag” correction: subtract 0.5–1.0% per event day if supply net < -10.
